plan.focus: Temescal's five businesses are all growing on paper, but the story is whether that growth reaches the people who actually live and work on the block — or whether it's just the ledger getting fatter while the sidewalk stays the same.
plan.closeQuestion: If every business on the block is growing, why does it still feel like the neighborhood is being pulled in two directions?

subjects.name: Bobby Chen-Ramirez
subjects.profile: Bobby Chen-Ramirez — Health Center Project Director — Temescal Community Health Center, Temescal

sources.name: Bobby Chen-Ramirez
sources.quote: Look, I run a health center project, not a spreadsheet. But I walk that block every day, and I see the same thing you're describing — the numbers on the wall don't mean a damn thing if Mrs. Okafor still can't get her blood pressure checked without taking two buses. What creates accountability for me is simple: I've got 14 employees on my roster, and every one of them lives in this neighborhood. When I see hiring signs in every storefront on the Jack London corridor, I want to know who's actually getting those jobs — is it the kid who grew up here, or is it somebody who commutes in from the hills? That's the story. That's what I want answered. Because if growth just means the ledger gets fatter while the sidewalk stays the same, then we're building a ghost town with good accounting.
